SwingTrade · Trade Plan Mechanics

How Stop, T1 & T2 Get Calculated

A plain-English, step-by-step walkthrough of exactly how the engine decides where you get out for a loss, and where you take profit — built for a brand-new trader.

Reward ≥ 3 × Risk
The golden rule baked into everything. No trade is allowed unless the profit target is worth at least 3× what you're risking. That's why the stop is always computed first — it defines your risk, and the target has to beat it 3-to-1.

First, one word you need: ATR.  ATR = Average True Range = how much a stock moves in a typical day. A $50 stock might have an ATR of $1.50. The engine never says "stop 3% away" — it says "stop 1.25 ATRs away," so the math automatically adapts to each stock's own volatility. ATR is the universal ruler.

1

Find the Entry zone

anchor = entry_mid

The engine doesn't pick one entry price — it builds a small zone around the current price, then uses the middle of that zone as the anchor for every other number.

entry_low = price − 0.30 × ATR entry_high = price + 0.20 × ATR entry_mid = (entry_low + entry_high) / 2 ← the anchor everything else hangs off

2

Set the Stop — your "I'm wrong" line

defines 1R

The single most important number. Base formula:

stop = entry_mid − (1.25 × ATR)

That 1.25 (the stop_atr_multiple in config) is the sweet spot: wide enough that normal daily wiggle won't knock you out, tight enough to cut a real loser fast. Then three real-trader refinements kick in:

  • Regime check — in a bear market the stop tightens to 1.0× ATR. When the odds are against you, bleed less. (line 6745)
  • Confluence snap — it nudges the stop onto a nearby Fibonacci level or the EMA50 moving average. Place your stop just under a line the market already respects, not a random price. (line 6794)
  • Fractal-low check — a "fractal low" is a recent swing bottom the market bounced off. If your stop sits above it, it's too tight (a normal dip stops you out), so the stop widens to just below that swing low. (line 6822)
Some setups override this. An EMA21 Pullback uses a tight fixed 1.5% stop — the data showed its winners bounce immediately and losers crater, so a tight stop cheaply kills the bad trades. (line 6859)
risk (a.k.a. 1R) = entry_mid − stop ← every target below is measured in multiples of this
3

Set the Targets — T1 and T2

2 engines

There are two ways the engine can place targets. Yours currently runs the smart one (use_structural_targets is ON).

A · Simple method (fallback)

Pure risk-multiples:

T1 = entry_mid + 3 × risk T2 = entry_mid + 5 × risk

One sanity check: if a resistance ceiling sits closer than 3R, T1 is placed just below it — no point aiming past a wall the stock can't break. (line 6836)

B · Structural engine (live)

Instead of blind multiples, it finds real overhead price levels where the stock is likely to stall, and aims there. Candidate sources:

FRACTALPrior swing-high peaks
HVN / VAHVolume walls & magnets
AVWAPFrom 52w-high / earnings
FIB EXT1.272× / 1.618× of swing
ROUND #$50, $100 psych levels
ELLIOTTWave-3 objectives

When several of those levels stack at the same price, that price scores higher confluence = a stronger target. The selector then picks:

  • T1 = highest-confluence level that's at least the minimum R away (so R:R still clears the 3:1 floor)
  • T2 = the next strong level beyond T1
  • T3 = optional "bull-stretch" reach target beyond T2
target_engine.py · select_targets() · line 1103
⛔ The overhead-supply gate. T1 is never allowed to leapfrog a wall. If there's a clear double-top or supply zone between your entry and a far-away juicy target, T1 gets pinned below that wall. You don't set a target on the other side of a brick wall. (target_engine.py line 173)

If the engine can't find clean structure, it silently falls back to the 3R / 5R math — the trade stays alive.

4

The R:R gate ties it together

pass / no-trade
R:R ratio = (T1 − entry_mid) / (entry_mid − stop)

If that number is below 3:1 (4:1 in risk-off regimes), the trade is not tradeable. This is the whole reason stop is computed first: the stop defines 1R, and T1 has to be worth at least 3 of them. (line 6854)

Putting it together — a worked example

$50 stock · ATR $1.50
REWARD · 3R+
RISK · 1R
$59.33 T2 · 5R runner
$55.57 T1 · 3R target
$49.93 ENTRY zone (mid)
$48.05 STOP · −1.25 ATR

Read it bottom-up

Stop $48.051.25 × $1.50 below entry. Risk = $1.88 per share = 1R.
Entry $49.93Middle of the entry zone — the anchor.
T1 $55.573 × $1.88 above entry → exactly 3:1. (Or nearest real wall.)
T2 $59.335 × risk — the runner you let ride.
StepCalculationValue
Entry mid(49.55 + 50.30) / 2$49.93
Stop49.93 − 1.25 × 1.50$48.05
Risk (1R)49.93 − 48.05$1.88
T1 (3R / nearest wall)49.93 + 3 × 1.88$55.57
T2 (5R / next wall)49.93 + 5 × 1.88$59.33

With structural targets ON, T1/T2 shift to the nearest real overhead levels (a fractal high or volume wall near those prices) instead of the exact 3R/5R math — but the stop and the 3:1 minimum stay identical.

The one-sentence summary

Stop = entry − 1.25 ATR (then snapped to a real support level); that distance is "1R"; T1 must be ≥ 3R away (placed at the nearest real overhead level, never past a wall); T2 is the next level beyond it.
